secrets.headline: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun
secrets.kids: Zap! A bolt of lightning heats the air around it to about 50,000°F. That's about 5 times hotter than the outside of the Sun! The air gets so hot so fast that it explodes outward, and that BOOM you hear is thunder!
secrets.grown: A lightning channel briefly heats the surrounding air to roughly 50,000°F (about 30,000 K), around five times the temperature of the Sun's visible surface. The sudden expansion of that superheated air is the thunder we hear. The Sun's core is far hotter; the comparison is with its surface.
pointers: The bolt heats the air to about 50,000°F

sources.title: National Weather Service: Lightning temperature
NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory: Lightning

secrets.headline: Some bamboo can grow almost 3 feet in one day
secrets.kids: Ready, set, GROW! Some kinds of bamboo can shoot up 35 inches in just one day. That's almost as tall as a yardstick, in a single day! And guess what? Bamboo isn't a tree at all. It's a giant grass!
secrets.grown: Guinness World Records lists certain bamboo species as the world's fastest-growing plants, at up to 91 cm (35 in) per day. Bamboo belongs to the grass family (Poaceae), with around 1,000 species.
pointers: Can grow up to 35 inches in a day

secrets.headline: Do big trees feed their babies through an underground fungus network?
secrets.claim: Big "mother trees" feed their baby trees through an underground fungus network.
secrets.kids: Partly true! Down under the forest floor, tiny fungus threads really do hook onto tree roots and trade food with them, like an underground swap shop. But the famous story that big "mother trees" feed their baby trees? Scientists who checked say the proof is still pretty thin. Sometimes the trees even compete!
secrets.grown: Mycorrhizal fungi do link tree roots, trading nutrients for carbon. But a 2023 review in New Phytologist found that the evidence for the "mother tree" hypothesis (big trees deliberately supplying seedlings through the network) is limited, and that the network can even increase competition between trees. A separate 2023 review in Nature Ecology & Evolution raised similar doubts.
pointers: Fungus threads link roots underground

sources.title: EurekAlert! (IIASA): Exploring the underground connections between trees
Newswise: Re-examining the mother tree hypothesis

secrets.headline: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood
secrets.kids: Count 'em: one, two, THREE hearts! Two of an octopus's hearts pump blood through its gills to grab oxygen. The third one pumps blood to the rest of its body. And get this: octopus blood is BLUE, because it uses copper instead of iron to carry oxygen!
secrets.grown: Octopuses have two branchial hearts that push blood through the gills and one systemic heart that circulates it through the body. Their blood uses the copper-based protein hemocyanin rather than iron-based hemoglobin, which gives it a blue color.
pointers: 2 hearts pump blood through the gills
1 heart pumps blood to the body

sources.title: BBC Science Focus: How many hearts does an octopus have?
Live Science: How many hearts does an octopus have?

secrets.headline: Bats hang upside down without using their muscles
secrets.kids: Hang on... or actually, don't! When a bat relaxes, special tendons lock its toes and claws in place, so hanging upside down takes zero effort. To let go, it has to use its muscles! Hanging up high also lets a bat just drop and fly away.
secrets.grown: A bat's talons work opposite to most muscles: when the bat relaxes, specialized tendons lock its toes in place, and body weight plus gravity keep it hanging without spending energy. Roosting upside down also lets bats launch by simply dropping into flight.
pointers: Tendons lock the claws, with no effort needed

sources.title: Iowa Department of Natural Resources: Why do bats hang upside down?
Live Science: Why do bats hang upside down to sleep?

secrets.headline: Do butterflies die right after laying their eggs?
secrets.claim: Butterflies die right after they lay their eggs.
secrets.kids: Busted! Adult monarch butterflies live about 2 to 6 weeks, and the moms lay eggs during most of that time. They die when they get old, and many still have eggs left. Some monarchs, the ones that migrate, can even live for months!
secrets.grown: According to monarch researcher Dr. Karen Oberhauser (Journey North), summer adult monarchs live about 2 to 6 weeks, and females lay eggs throughout most of that period. They die of old age, often with eggs still in their bodies. The migratory generation lives much longer, from about August or September until spring.
pointers: Adults live about 2 to 6 weeks

sources.title: Journey North: Monarch life cycle Q&A

secrets.headline: Mount Everest is NOT the closest place to space
secrets.kids: Surprise! Earth isn't a perfect ball. It's a little chubby around the middle, at the Equator. Mount Chimborazo in Ecuador sits right on that bulge, so its top is more than 6,800 feet farther from Earth's center than the top of Everest!
secrets.grown: Everest is highest above sea level, but because Earth bulges at the Equator, the summit of Ecuador's Mount Chimborazo is the farthest point on Earth's surface from the planet's center: more than 6,800 feet (2,072 m) farther out than Everest's summit, according to NOAA.
pointers: The farthest point from Earth's center

sources.title: NOAA Ocean Service: What is the highest point on Earth as measured from Earth's center?
Library of Congress: Farthest point from the center of the Earth

secrets.headline: The Sahara Desert used to be green
secrets.kids: Picture the biggest hot desert on Earth... now picture it GREEN! Thousands of years ago, the Sahara had lakes, grasslands and animals that need lots of water. Tiny changes in the way Earth wobbles around the Sun brought more rain. Scientists find the clues in ancient pollen and mud from the ocean floor.
secrets.grown: During the African Humid Period, which peaked between about 9,000 and 6,000 years ago, North Africa was far wetter, with lakes and vegetation. It was driven by African monsoon responses to cyclical changes in Earth's orbit that recur roughly every 20,000 years. Evidence includes deep-sea sediment cores and ancient pollen.
pointers: This desert once had lakes and grassland

sources.title: Nature Education (Scitable): Green Sahara, African Humid Periods paced by Earth's orbital changes

secrets.headline: Days on Earth are slowly getting longer
secrets.kids: Brake check! The Moon's pull makes ocean tides, and those tides work like a tiny brake on Earth's spin. Every 100 years, a day gets about 2 thousandths of a second longer. Want a 25-hour day? You'd have to wait about 200 million years!
secrets.grown: Tidal friction from the Moon (and Sun) gradually slows Earth's rotation. Estimates put the lengthening at about 1.7 to 2.3 milliseconds per century, so a 25-hour day is on the order of 200 million years away. Other factors, like shifting ice and the planet's core, also nudge day length up and down.
pointers: Tides act like a slow brake on Earth's spin

sources.title: Scientific American: Fact or fiction, the days are getting longer
EarthDate: The day's getting longer

secrets.headline: Most of the ocean has never been explored
secrets.kids: Calling all explorers! Scientists say about 80% of the ocean is still unmapped and unexplored. There are underwater mountains, canyons and places no person has ever seen. The biggest mystery might be right here on Earth!
secrets.grown: NOAA has long described roughly 80% of the ocean as "unmapped, unobserved, and unexplored." Mapping is improving, so the exact numbers keep shifting; in U.S. waters alone, about 44% of the seafloor remained unmapped at modern standards as of January 2026. Seeing the deep ocean directly is rarer still.
pointers: Most of the deep ocean has never been seen

sources.title: NOAA Ocean Exploration: How much of the ocean has been explored?
NOAA Office of Coast Survey: U.S. continues to close mapping gaps

secrets.headline: Mount Everest would vanish in the deepest part of the ocean
secrets.kids: Big mountain, BIGGER hole! The Challenger Deep in the Pacific Ocean is about 35,876 feet deep. If you set Mount Everest on the bottom, there would still be more than a mile of water above its peak!
secrets.grown: The Challenger Deep, at the southern end of the Mariana Trench, is about 35,876 ft (10,935 m) deep by NOAA's estimate. Mount Everest rises 29,032 ft above sea level, so placed on the bottom, its summit would sit more than a mile underwater.
pointers: The deepest known point in the ocean

sources.title: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information: The Challenger Deep
Live Science: How deep is the Mariana Trench?

secrets.headline: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean
secrets.kids: Take a deep breath... and thank the ocean! Tiny drifting living things called plankton make oxygen, just like trees do. There are so many of them that together they make about half of the oxygen on Earth!
secrets.grown: NOAA estimates that about half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, mostly from photosynthetic plankton near the surface. Marine life also consumes about the same amount, and most of the oxygen we breathe has built up in the atmosphere over hundreds of millions of years.
pointers: Tiny plankton make oxygen

secrets.headline: A day on Venus is longer than its year
secrets.kids: Happy birthday... before bedtime? Venus spins super slowly. One full spin takes 243 Earth days, but one trip around the Sun takes only about 225. So on Venus, a day lasts longer than a whole year!
secrets.grown: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once on its axis (its sidereal day) but only about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. One nuance: because Venus spins backward, the time from one sunrise to the next is about 117 Earth days.
pointers: One spin takes 243 Earth days

sources.title: Snopes (quoting NASA): One day on Venus is longer than a year

secrets.headline: Astronaut footprints are still on the Moon
secrets.kids: Footprints that last (almost) forever! The Moon has no wind or rain to wash footprints away. Tiny space rocks slowly stir up the dust, but so slowly that the astronauts' footprints should last at least a million years!
secrets.grown: With no atmosphere, wind or water, the Moon lacks the forces that erase footprints on Earth. The main eraser is "impact gardening" by tiny micrometeorites, which is slow enough that the Apollo footprints should last at least a million years, per the American Museum of Natural History.
pointers: No wind or rain to erase them

sources.title: American Museum of Natural History: On the Moon
Space.com: Flags and footprints of Apollo astronauts won't last forever

secrets.headline: Can you see the Great Wall of China from space?
secrets.claim: You can see the Great Wall of China from space with your eyes.
secrets.kids: Busted! The Great Wall is super long, but it's narrow, and it's about the same color as the land around it. Astronauts say they can't spot it with just their eyes from orbit, and you definitely can't see it from the Moon.
secrets.grown: NASA describes this as a space-based myth: the wall generally isn't visible to the unaided eye from low Earth orbit, and it isn't visible from the Moon. It's narrow and blends with its surroundings. Astronaut Leroy Chiao did photograph it from the ISS in 2004, but with a zoom lens.
pointers: Long, but narrow and land-colored

sources.title: NASA (archived): China's Wall less great in view from space
Britannica: Can you see the Great Wall of China from space?

secrets.headline: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid
secrets.kids: Time-travel brain twister! The Great Pyramid was finished around 2560 BC. Cleopatra lived about 2,500 years later, and the Moon landing in 1969 came only about 2,000 years after her. To Cleopatra, the pyramids were already ancient!
secrets.grown: The Great Pyramid of Giza was completed around 2560 BC. Cleopatra VII died in 30 BC, roughly 2,500 years later, while the 1969 Apollo 11 landing came about 2,000 years after her death.
pointers: Already about 2,500 years old in Cleopatra's time

sources.title: WorldAtlas: Did Cleopatra really live closer in time to the first lunar landing than the Great Pyramids?

secrets.headline: Was Napoleon really short?
secrets.kids: Busted! His height was written down as 5 feet 2 inches, but in old French inches, which were longer than ours. In today's inches he was about 5 feet 7, a little taller than the average Frenchman back then. Measuring mix-up solved!
secrets.grown: Napoleon's recorded height of 5 feet 2 inches was in French units, which were longer than British ones. Converted, he was about 5 feet 6 or 7 inches, roughly average or slightly above average for a Frenchman of his time.
pointers: About 5 feet 7 in today's inches

secrets.headline: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
secrets.kids: School has been in session a LONG time! People were already teaching at Oxford in England by the year 1096. The Aztec capital city, Tenochtitlán, wasn't founded until about 1325, more than 200 years later!
secrets.grown: Oxford has no exact founding date, but teaching existed there by at least 1096. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlán was founded around 1325, and the empire itself took shape in 1428, so Oxford predates both.
pointers: Teaching here began by 1096

sources.title: Britannica: What university is older than the Aztec Empire?

secrets.headline: Why does a plug have a third prong?
secrets.kids: Meet the plug's bodyguard! The round third prong is called the "ground." If something goes wrong inside a machine, it gives stray electricity a safe path into the ground instead of through you. That's why you should never cut it off!
secrets.grown: A two-prong plug carries current through the hot and neutral wires. The third, round prong is the ground: it connects an appliance's metal casing to the building's grounding wire, giving fault current a safe path to earth instead of through a person. Removing it defeats the safety feature.
pointers: The round prong is the safety ground

sources.title: ScienceABC: When does an appliance need a 3-pronged plug?
Sciencing: How does a 3-pin plug work?

secrets.headline: The microwave oven was discovered by accident
secrets.kids: Oops... INVENTION! In 1945, an engineer named Percy Spencer was working near radar equipment when the snack in his pocket melted. Next he tried popcorn kernels, and they popped all over his lab! That led to the microwave oven. People still argue about which candy bar it was!
secrets.grown: Raytheon engineer Percy Spencer noticed that a candy bar in his pocket heated up while he stood near a magnetron, the tube that produces microwave energy. He then tested popcorn kernels, which popped, and the work led to the first microwave oven. Accounts differ on the exact snack, and the heating effect of microwave tubes was already somewhat known; Spencer's contribution was turning it into a cooking device.
pointers: Started with a melted snack in 1945

sources.title: IEEE Spectrum: A history of the microwave oven
Invention & Technology: The greatest discovery since fire

secrets.headline: Was the QWERTY keyboard made to slow typists down?
secrets.claim: The QWERTY keyboard was designed to slow typists down.
secrets.kids: Mostly a myth! Early typewriters could jam, and the inventor moved the letters around many times. But slowing people down wasn't the goal, and historians still argue about why the keys ended up where they are. Lots of common letter pairs, like "er" and "th," still sit close together!
secrets.grown: The popular story says Christopher Sholes scrambled the keys to slow typists and prevent jams. Historians are skeptical: Sholes wanted fast typing without jams, many common letter pairs still sit near each other, and research by Koichi and Motoko Yasuoka points to other influences, such as early telegraph operators. The layout became standard in 1893 when major manufacturers merged.
pointers: Q-W-E-R-T-Y: the first six letters on the top row

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine: Fact or fiction? The legend of the QWERTY keyboard

secrets.headline: Babies have more bones than grown-ups
secrets.kids: Babies are bone champions! A baby is born with around 300 bones. As kids grow, some of those bones fuse, which means they join together. By the time you're grown up, you'll have 206.
secrets.grown: Newborns have roughly 270 to 300 bony elements, many still partly cartilage. Through childhood and adolescence many of them fuse, settling at the familiar adult count of about 206.
pointers: Adults have 206 bones

sources.title: Healthline: How many bones does a baby have?
Live Science: Surprising facts about the skeletal system

secrets.headline: You're taller in the morning than at night
secrets.kids: Good morning, taller you! The soft cushions between the bones in your back, called discs, are full of water. Standing up all day squishes them a little, so you shrink, about half an inch! At night, lying down lets them plump back up.
secrets.grown: Intervertebral discs are mostly water. Upright activity during the day compresses them, and lying down at night lets fluid diffuse back in, so most people are measurably taller in the morning. A parson measured a loss of up to about 15 mm (0.6 in) over a day back in 1724; in medieval France, army recruits reportedly applied in the morning to appear taller.
pointers: Water-filled discs squeeze down during the day

sources.title: Indiana Public Media, A Moment of Science: Overnight results
NZ Herald (citing New Scientist): Is it true we are taller in the morning?

secrets.headline: Do we only use 10% of our brain?
secrets.claim: We only use 10% of our brain.
secrets.kids: Busted! Brain scans show we use virtually every part of our brain, and most of it is busy almost all the time. Your brain is only about 3% of your body's weight, but it gobbles up about 20% of your energy!
secrets.grown: Neurologists call the 10% claim a myth. Brain-imaging studies have consistently failed to find any region that is perpetually inactive, and damage to almost any area has effects. The brain is about 3% of body weight yet uses about 20% of the body's energy.
pointers: Virtually every part is used
